title: Title and date
short: Walton said Donne wrote it eight days before his death in March 1631; a manuscript dates it to his illness of December 1623.
body: Izaak Walton, Donne's first biographer, dated the hymn 23 March 1630 (1631 in modern reckoning), eight days before Donne's death. A copy among the papers of Sir Julius Caesar says it was written in Donne's 'great sickness in December 1623', the illness that produced the Devotions upon Emergent Occasions. Grierson weighed both and inclined to Walton; G. C. Moore Smith, Gardner and most later scholars favour 1623. The poem was first printed in 1635. The title's doubled 'God my God' recalls the Psalms (e.g. Psalm 22:1, 'My God, my God').

title: that Holy roome
short: Heaven, pictured as a room where the choir of saints sings, with the sickroom as its antechamber.
body: The speaker is at the door of heaven. The 'Holy roome' contrasts with the room in which he lies sick, and the whole first stanza turns on this threshold. Walton, who dates the poem to Donne's last illness, tells how Donne posed in his shroud for the drawing from which his monument in St Paul's was carved; Grierson adds that Donne designed the monument himself and that its epitaph is the natural supplement to the hymn.

title: Quire of Saints ... I shall be made thy Musique
short: In heaven he will become part of God's music, joined to the choir of saints.
body: Endicott glosses 'thy Musique' as God's company of musicians: the speaker will not only sing but become music. The image draws on Revelation's heavenly choirs (Revelation 5:8-9, 14:2-3) and on the old idea of the soul as a harmony. 'Quire' is the usual seventeenth-century spelling of 'choir'. The future tense ('I shall be made') makes heaven a transformation rather than a destination: the singer becomes the song. Donne often wrote of the soul's harmony with God, and the image prepares for the tuning of the next line.

sources.cite: N. J. Endicott, notes to 'Hymn to God, My God, in my Sickness', Representative Poetry Online (University of Toronto), l. 3
Bible (KJV), Revelation 14:2-3

title: I tune the Instrument here at the dore
short: Like a musician tuning before entering, he prepares his soul (and this poem) for heaven.
body: Musicians tuned their instruments outside the chamber before playing. The instrument is the speaker himself, body and soul, and the poem is his tuning. The last line of the stanza makes the poem a meditation in advance: 'what I must doe then, thinke here before'. The musical image also recalls Herbert's habit of figuring devotion as tuning, as in 'The Temper'.

title: my Physitians ... Cosmographers, and I their Mapp
short: The doctors bent over him become map-makers, and his body, lying flat, is their map.
body: Cosmographers described and mapped the world. The physicians poring over the patient are pictured as geographers studying a chart. Grierson adds that Sir Julius Caesar's manuscript reads 'by their Loer' (lore, learning) instead of 'by their love', which he thought probably the true reading; most editors keep 'love'. The map conceit governs the next three stanzas. The love of the physicians makes them attentive readers of his body.

sources.cite: H. J. C. Grierson, ed., The Poems of John Donne (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1912), vol. 2, commentary, p. 368 and Addendum, note to l. 6

title: my South-west discoverie
short: His discovery of the south-west: south for the heat of fever, west for the setting sun of death.
body: On the map of his body, the fever's heat is the hot south, and death is the west, where the sun sets. Voyages of discovery in Donne's lifetime sought routes to the Pacific through the south-west, by the Straits of Magellan. The doctors' examination therefore shows that he is about to make the final voyage. The pun on 'discovery' (revelation, uncovering) adds a medical sense.

sources.cite: A. J. Smith, ed., John Donne: The Complete English Poems (Harmondsworth: Penguin, 1971), notes to the poem

title: Per fretum febris
short: Latin: 'through the strait of fever'. 'Fretum' also suggests heat and turbulence.
body: Endicott translates the phrase as 'through the straits of fever' and notes the pun on 'straits', meaning both narrow sea passages and hardships. Ancient etymologists connected fretum with fervere, to boil, so the word may also suggest the burning of fever. The Latin also gives the line a ceremonial, inscription-like quality, as if it were a legend on a map.

title: straits
short: A pun: 'straits' are both narrow sea passages and distressing difficulties.
body: The ordinary sense of 'in great straits' (in hardship) meets the geographical one. The sick man is in straits; but straits, as navigators knew, lead to oceans. Grierson quotes sermons in which Donne uses the same figure: a narrower way, but to a better land, through straits to the Pacific Sea. The pain of sickness is thus the passage to his 'home'.

title: I see my West
short: He rejoices to see his west, his death, approaching.
body: The west, where the sun sets, is the conventional region of death. The surprise is 'I joy': the sight of death is not fearful because, as the next lines argue, west and east meet. The phrase may also glance at the sea-currents of the Straits of Magellan, which ran westward so strongly that ships could not return ('theire currants yeeld returne to none').

title: theire currants yeeld returne to none
short: The currents of the straits allow no voyage back, as no one returns from death.
body: Contemporary accounts described the Straits of Magellan as hard to pass eastward because of currents and winds. The image fuses this sailor's knowledge with the proverbial 'undiscovered country, from whose bourn no traveller returns' (Hamlet). The fact that there is no return is accepted with equanimity, since the voyage has a happy end. Grierson cites Hakluyt's Principal Navigations for the geography of the straits.

sources.cite: A. J. Smith, ed., John Donne: The Complete English Poems (Harmondsworth: Penguin, 1971), notes to the poem

title: As West and East / In all flatt Maps ... are one
short: On a flat map pasted onto a globe, the far west and far east meet; so death touches resurrection.
body: On a flat map the extreme east and west edges represent the same meridian. Donne used the figure in a sermon on Psalm 6, quoted by Grierson: paste a flat map on a round body and west and east are all one. In the same sermon he recalls that one of Christ's names is Oriens, 'the East' (Zechariah 6:12 in the Vulgate), so that death's west becomes Christ's east. His epitaph in St Paul's says he looks toward him whose name is the Rising. The parenthesis '(and I am one)' makes the speaker himself a flat map, lying on his bed.

title: So death doth touch the Resurrection
short: Just as west meets east, death meets and touches resurrection; they are one point on the map.
body: The stanza's conclusion is a theological claim made through geography. 'Touch' is precise: on the globe the two edges are contiguous. The line also echoes the Christian tradition of burying the dead facing east, toward the rising sun and the expected return of Christ, which Grierson illustrates from Walton's account of Donne's monument, turned to the east. The conclusion is stated as calmly as a geometrical proof.

title: the Pacifique Sea ... The Easterne riches ... Ierusalem
short: Three possible 'homes': the peaceful ocean, the wealth of the East Indies, and Jerusalem, the heavenly city.
body: Each destination is also a figure for heaven: the Pacific is the sea of peace (Latin pacificus); the 'Easterne riches' are the spices and treasures of the Moluccas and the Far East; Jerusalem is the earthly city and the New Jerusalem of Revelation 21. Grierson explains that, on the maps of the period, each could be reached only through a strait.

Bible (KJV), Revelation 21:2

title: Anyan, Magellan, Gibraltare
short: Three straits: Anian (thought to separate America from Asia), Magellan, and Gibraltar.
body: Grierson explains the condensed syntax: whether his home is the Pacific, the East or Jerusalem, it is reached through a strait. The Strait of Anian, a supposed passage between America and Asia, is often identified with the Bering Strait (Endicott glosses it so); maps in Hakluyt show it leading to Japan and the Moluccas. Magellan's strait, at the tip of South America, leads to the Pacific; Gibraltar leads to the Mediterranean and Jerusalem. Grierson rejects Grosart's and Chambers's emendations of the line and notes that Donne uses the geography of his youth.

anchor: Iaphet dwelt, or Cham, or Sem
title: Japhet, Ham, Shem
short: Noah's three sons, traditionally the ancestors of the peoples of Europe, Africa and Asia.
body: Genesis 10 traces the nations of the earth to Shem, Ham and Japheth; by tradition Japheth's descendants peopled Europe, Ham's Africa and Shem's Asia. The line thus maps the three straits and three destinations onto the three continents of the old world, so that all the known world is gathered into the speaker's voyage. The early modern division of the world among Noah's sons was a commonplace of maps and universal histories. Each continent, like each strait, becomes a way to the one destination, so that the whole of human geography points toward heaven.

title: Paradise and Calvarie, / Christs Crosse, and Adams tree
short: An old tradition held that Christ was crucified where Eden's tree stood, or where Adam was buried.
body: Patristic and medieval legend placed Golgotha ('the place of a skull') over Adam's grave, and some traditions said the wood of the cross came from the tree of Eden. Endicott notes that no source gives a precise identification of Paradise with Calvary, though such linking of biblical places was common in early commentary, and that 'place' may mean region. The tradition supports the typology of the next lines.

title: both Adams
short: Adam, whose sin brought death, and Christ, the 'last Adam', who brought life, meet in the dying speaker.
body: Paul calls Christ 'the last Adam' (1 Corinthians 15:45) and says 'as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive' (15:22; compare Romans 5:12-19). The first Adam's curse was to eat bread 'in the sweat of thy face' (Genesis 3:19); the sick man's fever-sweat is that curse. The last Adam's blood, shed on the cross, will 'embrace' his soul. Christ's own sweat 'as it were great drops of blood' in Gethsemane (Luke 22:44) links the two.

title: in his purple wrapp'd
short: Wrapped in Christ's purple, the robe the soldiers mocked him with, which is also his blood and royal dignity.
body: At the Passion the soldiers put on Jesus 'a purple robe' and a crown of thorns (John 19:2). Purple is royal, and it is also the colour of blood, so the speaker asks to be wrapped in Christ's blood and kingship. 'Wrapp'd' suggests the shroud as well, recalling Walton's account of Donne posing in his winding-sheet. The colour thus unites mockery, kingship, blood and burial in a single word.

title: By these his thornes give me his other Crowne
short: Through sharing Christ's crown of thorns (his sufferings), he hopes for Christ's other crown, of glory.
body: The crown of thorns (John 19:2) is set against 'a crown of righteousness' (2 Timothy 4:8) and 'the crown of life' promised to those who endure temptation (James 1:12). Suffering is the condition of glory: the sickness that makes him share the thorns is the way to the other crown. The two crowns sum up the poem's logic of opposites meeting: thorns and glory, west and east, the first and the last Adam. 'These his thornes' identifies the speaker's present pains with Christ's.

sources.cite: Bible (KJV), 2 Timothy 4:8
Bible (KJV), James 1:12

title: Be this my Text, my Sermon to mine owne
short: The preacher who preached God's word to others now preaches to his own soul, with this verse as his text.
body: Donne had been Dean of St Paul's since 1621 and was the most celebrated preacher of his age. A sermon begins with a text from Scripture; here the 'text' is the sentence that follows, the poem's last line, which reads like a biblical maxim. The turn inward ('mine owne' soul) gathers the poem's public images into private application. The speaker becomes both preacher and congregation.

title: Therfore that he may raise the Lord throws down
short: God casts down so that he may raise up: an idea from Scripture, compressed into a line that itself falls and rises.
body: The idea is biblical: 'The LORD killeth, and maketh alive: he bringeth down to the grave, and bringeth up' (1 Samuel 2:6; compare Psalm 146:8, 'the LORD raiseth them that are bowed down'). Grierson compares a phrase from the Devotions: cast down so as not to be cast away. The inverted syntax places 'raise' before 'throws down', so that the sentence reverses the order of events and ends on the fall, which the reader knows is temporary. The stanza form, five pentameter lines rhyming ababb, closes the poem on its rhyme with 'Crowne'.
